title: Kanem-Bornu: kings on both sides of Lake Chad
intro: Kanem grew up north-east of Lake Chad. In the late 1300s its kings left for Bornu, west of the lake, in today's north-eastern Nigeria, and their line, the Sayfawa, ruled there until 1846. Most early dates come from the royal chronicle, the girgam, written down long after the events, and from later histories. Many of them differ, and are labelled where they do. The sources for this chapter have so far been read only in short excerpts and still need checking against the full texts.

features.name: Lake Chad
features.what: The lake between Kanem, to its north-east, and Bornu, to its west. It was never a fixed shape. Its level rose and fell over these centuries; a small lake in the Bodélé depression, north-east of today's lake, dried out only about 1,000 years ago; and since the 1960s the lake has shrunk to less than a tenth of its area then.
features.location: The dot marks today's lake, and the background draws today's outline. That is not the shoreline of any period in this chapter; no older shoreline is drawn, because none has been sourced.

features.name: Kanem
features.what: The first heartland of the kingdom, north-east of Lake Chad. Its capital, Njimi, has never been securely located. Archaeologists working at Tié have proposed it as a probable site of Njimi.
features.evidence: Secondary sources, qualified by recent archaeological research
features.location: A regional anchor at today's Mao, not a capital. Njimi is not placed, and Tié's exact position has not been checked for this page. The ring marks the region.
features.disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700, but some sources give about 600 or about 900.

features.name: Bilma (Kawar)
features.what: An oasis of Kawar in the Sahara, where rock salt was mined. Caravans carried it south to the savanna north of Lake Chad.

features.name: Salt road from Bilma to Kanem
features.what: The shortest crossing of the Sahara: salt went south from Bilma, and enslaved people and ivory went north in exchange, on the road to Tripoli by way of Murzuk.
features.location: A line between the two places. The caravans' track across the dunes is not drawn.

features.name: Bulala (Lake Fitri)
features.what: The Bulala (Bilala) came from the lands around Lake Fitri, east of Kanem. In the late 1300s they drove the Sayfawa kings out of Kanem and ruled it until about 1630, when they lost it and settled around Lake Fitri.
features.location: Drawn at Lake Fitri. Where the Bulala rulers sat while they held Kanem is not placed.

features.name: Ngazargamu (Birni Gazargamo)
features.what: Bornu's capital, built by Mai Ali Gaji between the Komadugu Gana and the Komadugu Yobe rivers. It was the first lasting capital after Njimi was lost, and it stood until the Fulani took and destroyed it in 1808.
features.location: The ruins near today's Geidam, Yobe State. The point is the capital; how far Bornu reached is not drawn.
features.disputed: Ngazargamu's founding is dated about 1460, about 1462, by 1472 and about 1488 in different sources.

features.name: Kukawa
features.what: Founded as Kuka in 1814 by Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, as his own seat, after he helped restore the mai.
features.location: Today's town of Kukawa, Borno State.

features.name: The Kanembu move west to Bornu
features.what: Driven out by the Bulala, Mai Umar ibn Idris left Njimi and led the Kanembu west to Bornu. For decades after that the court had no lasting seat, until Ngazargamu was built.
features.location: Schematic: from the Kanem region to the land west of the lake. The way they went, and where the court stopped before Ngazargamu, are not drawn.

scenes.title: Kanem, north-east of Lake Chad
scenes.text: Kanem grew up north-east of Lake Chad. Its founding is usually dated about 700, though some sources say about 600 or about 900. Its old capital, Njimi, has never been securely found; archaeologists have proposed Tié, which is not placed here. Caravans brought rock salt south from Bilma, and Kanem sent ivory and enslaved people north. The lake was not the lake on today's maps. Its level rose and fell over these centuries, and its shores moved with it.
scenes.disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700, but some sources give about 600 or about 900.

beats.text: Kanem grew up north-east of Lake Chad.
Its founding is usually dated about 700, though some sources say about 600 or about 900.
Its old capital, Njimi, has never been securely found; archaeologists have proposed Tié, which is not placed here.
Caravans brought rock salt south from Bilma, and Kanem sent ivory and enslaved people north.
The lake was not the lake on today's maps.
Its level rose and fell over these centuries, and its shores moved with it.

scenes.title: The Sayfawa kings
scenes.text: In the late 1000s a new line of kings, the Sayfawa, began with Hummay. His dates differ: towards 1068, 1075 to 1086, or 1085 to 1097. The royal chronicle makes him the son of the king before him. The historian Dierk Lange reads his rise as a change of dynasty, not the first turn to Islam. In the 1200s Mai Dunama Dibalemi took Kanem's power north along the caravan roads, to Kawar and the Fezzan. After his death his sons fought each other, and outlying peoples stopped paying tribute.
scenes.disputed: Hummay's rise is dated towards 1068, 1075-1086 or 1085-1097, and whether it marks a conversion to Islam or a change of dynasty is debated. Dunama Dibalemi's reign is given as 1210-1259 or 1221-1259.

beats.text: In the late 1000s a new line of kings, the Sayfawa, began with Hummay.
His dates differ: towards 1068, 1075 to 1086, or 1085 to 1097.
The royal chronicle makes him the son of the king before him.
The historian Dierk Lange reads his rise as a change of dynasty, not the first turn to Islam.
In the 1200s Mai Dunama Dibalemi took Kanem's power north along the caravan roads, to Kawar and the Fezzan.

scenes.title: From Kanem to Bornu
scenes.text: From around Lake Fitri, to the east, came the Bulala. By one account they killed five of the six kings who reigned between 1376 and 1400. Mai Umar ibn Idris left Njimi and led the Kanembu west, to Bornu, on the far side of the lake. The move is dated from about 1380 to 1387. In Bornu the Kanembu married into the peoples already there, and from them came the Kanuri. For decades the court had no lasting seat. Then Mai Ali Gaji built Ngazargamu, between two rivers. Its founding is dated anywhere from about 1460 to 1488.
scenes.disputed: The Bulala are said to have taken Njimi in 1363 by one account, or to have driven the Sayfawa out by 1376 and taken Kanem by 1388 by another. The move to Bornu is dated about 1380 or about 1387, and Ngazargamu's founding from about 1460 to about 1488.

The move is dated from about 1380 to 1387.
In Bornu the Kanembu married into the peoples already there, and from them came the Kanuri.
For decades the court had no lasting seat.
Then Mai Ali Gaji built Ngazargamu, between two rivers.

scenes.title: Idris Alooma
scenes.text: Bornu was at its strongest under Mai Idris Alooma. Most sources give his reign as about 1571 to 1603; others begin it in 1564 or end it as late as 1617. His chief imam, Ahmad ibn Furtu, wrote its history, in praise of the king. Ibn Furtu tells of seven expeditions against the Bulala of Kanem, about 1573 to 1578. He counts Turkish musketeers, and enslaved men of the household trained to fire guns, among the king's strengths. It is the earliest mention of guns in the region, and how much they decided is debated. Idris also made the great men of the state live at his court, and bound them to him by marriage.
scenes.disputed: Idris Alooma's reign is given as about 1571-1603 by most sources checked, and as about 1564-1596, about 1570 to 1600-1617, and 1580-1619 by others. The main account of his wars is his own imam's, written in his praise.

beats.text: Bornu was at its strongest under Mai Idris Alooma.
Most sources give his reign as about 1571 to 1603; others begin it in 1564 or end it as late as 1617.
His chief imam, Ahmad ibn Furtu, wrote its history, in praise of the king.
Ibn Furtu tells of seven expeditions against the Bulala of Kanem, about 1573 to 1578.
He counts Turkish musketeers, and enslaved men of the household trained to fire guns, among the king's strengths.

scenes.title: The end of the Sayfawa
scenes.text: In 1808 Fulani warriors of the jihad took Ngazargamu and destroyed it, and the capital was abandoned. Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi fought to free it; many stories of his part were later embellished. In 1814 he helped restore the mai, and built his own seat at Kukawa. In 1846 Mai Ibrahim called in the army of Wadai against al-Kanemi's son Umar. Umar had Ibrahim seized, and by most accounts put to death. Ibrahim's son Ali, made mai by Wadai, died the same year. With him the Sayfawa line ended, after more than seven centuries. Al-Kanemi's descendants ruled Bornu until 1893.
scenes.disputed: Accounts of 1846 differ: one says Umar imprisoned Ibrahim, others that he executed him (some date this to 1847); Ali is said to have died at Minarge, or to have been defeated and killed by Umar within six weeks.
